turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, thank you for seeing me. It’s... it’s a little hard to put into words perfectly, but I’ve just been dealing with this constant, underlying restless feeling. It’s like I’m wound just way too tight, like a spring, you know? And I just can’t seem to fully settle down, no matter what I’m doing. 

I mean, I’m a retail buyer, so my day-to-day is pretty fast-paced, which you'd think would burn off that energy, but it doesn't. Even when I’m supposed to be completely calm, the feeling is still there. Like, we have these long vendor planning meetings at work, and I’m just sitting there feeling this hum of restlessness the entire time, just wanting to get out of my chair. And it bleeds into my personal time, too. I try to do things to relax—I love painting, I’ll set up my canvases on the weekend, or I’ll go to a yoga class because everyone always says yoga is so good for centering yourself and finding peace—but even then, right in the middle of a pose or while I'm trying to focus on a brushstroke, I can't fully settle. I'm just buzzing on the inside, wound up tight, and I really don't know why I can't just sit and be calm like everyone else seems to be able to do so effortlessly. It's just always there.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also find yourself worrying about many different things most days?

No, not really... it’s funny you ask that, actually, because people assume that all the time. My husband, for instance, he’ll see me pacing around the living room or shifting a million times on the couch, and he’ll ask, "What’s wrong? What are you stressing about?" And I always have to tell him, I’m not stressing about anything! 

I don't really sit around agonizing over things. I mean, sure, work is busy, and dealing with wholesale suppliers and shipping delays can be a total headache, but I don't take it home and fret over it. I don't lie awake at night spinning my wheels about finances or the state of the world or what someone said to me at the grocery store. My mind isn't filled with all these anxious "what ifs," you know? I've been a buyer for a long time, I know how to handle the curveballs. 

It’s really just this purely physical sensation. I can be in the best mood, completely content, painting a canvas and not having a single negative or worried thought in my head, but my foot is just going a mile a minute under the easel and I feel like I need to jump up and walk around the block. So, no, I wouldn't call myself a worrier at all. If anything, I'm usually the one telling my friends to stop overthinking things! Which just makes this whole buzzing feeling so much more frustrating, because if I was worried about something, at least there would be a logical reason for why I can't just sit still and relax, but since my mind is perfectly fine... I just don't get it.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have similar trouble sitting still or feeling restless when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. Yes, it’s not a new thing at all. Honestly, it goes way, way back. I mean, my mother saved all my old report cards and notes from teachers, and she actually just brought a box of them over a few months ago when she was downsizing. I was looking through them, and it’s almost comical how consistent it is. 

I remember specifically in elementary school—second grade, third grade, Mrs. Gable’s class, Mr. Henderson’s class—it was always the same story. They were constantly sending notes home to my parents. And it wasn't that I was a bad kid or malicious, it was just... I literally could not stay in my seat. I’d be up sharpening my pencil three times, or walking over to the reading corner when we were supposed to be doing math, just constantly popping out of my chair like I was spring-loaded. 

And the talking! Oh my goodness, the notes always mentioned the talking. I would just blurt things out. I’d be talking over my classmates, interrupting, because I just had so much energy and the thought would pop into my head and I just had to get it out right that second. I remember teachers would be halfway through asking a question—like, they hadn't even finished the sentence—and I’d be rushing to answer it, practically shouting it out before anyone else had a chance to even process what was being asked. My parents tried everything, reward charts, punishments, but I just... I couldn't contain it. So, yes, that restless, buzzing feeling has been with me for as long as I can remember, really. It just looks a little different now that I'm an adult in a boardroom instead of a kid on a classroom rug, but the internal feeling is exactly the same.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often have trouble sustaining your attention on tasks or activities, even when they’re important to do?
turns.patient_response:
No, actually, I don't really struggle with that. It's interesting, because I know people sometimes associate feeling restless with not being able to focus, but for me, those two things just don't go together. If I need to get something done, especially if it's important, I'm completely locked in. 

Like at work, for example. Being a buyer, you have to be so detail-oriented. I'll be looking at spreadsheets, analyzing sales trends for the last three quarters, comparing vendor pricing matrices, trying to figure out if we should increase our order volume on a specific product line for the holiday season... and I can sit there and just power through it. I don't lose my place, I don't get distracted and forget what I'm doing. My mind is totally focused on the numbers and the strategy. I mean, my body might be doing its own thing—like I said, my foot might be tapping a hole into the floorboard, or I might be clicking my pen a hundred times a minute, driving my assistant crazy—but my actual attention is right there on the screen. 

And it's the same thing at home. If I'm paying bills or reading a contract for some home repairs we're having done, I don't drift off. I read every line, I get it done. Even with my painting, which is supposed to be my relaxation time... I can focus on mixing the exact right shade of blue for the sky for twenty minutes straight. I don't lose my train of thought or forget what I was trying to accomplish. So, no, my attention span is actually really good. It's just my body that refuses to cooperate and stay still while my brain is doing all the focusing!

No, not really. I mean, I'm pretty organized, honestly. I have to be, with my job. You can't be a buyer for a major retail chain and be constantly misplacing your purchase orders or losing your vendor contacts, right? It would be a disaster. So, I have systems.

My husband and I have this beautiful little ceramic bowl right by the front door—we bought it on a trip to Santa Fe a few years ago, it has this gorgeous turquoise glaze—and the rule is, the minute you walk in, the keys go in the bowl. I'm just not one of those people who leaves their phone in the refrigerator or something crazy like that. I know some people are like that, and I always wonder how they function! Paperwork goes into the filing cabinet in the home office—I have it all color-coded by year and category, which probably sounds a little intense, but it saves so much time when tax season rolls around. So, no, I don't really lose things. I might be pacing around the house while I'm on a conference call, but I know exactly where my notes are.

turns.patient_response:
No, not that I can remember, and certainly not in those report cards I mentioned earlier. I mean, my mother and I sat at her kitchen table—she has this lovely little breakfast nook that looks out over her garden—and we went through practically every single piece of paper from kindergarten through, gosh, probably eighth grade. I knew exactly what the teacher was saying, which is why I'd blurt out the answers before she even finished asking the question! I wasn't daydreaming or staring out the window or forgetting what we were doing. I was just... doing it very loudly and with a lot of movement. I remember one time in fourth grade, we were doing a unit on the solar system, and I had built this whole diorama in a shoebox—painted the inside black, hung the little styrofoam planets from fishing line—and I was so focused on it, I practically memorized the encyclopedia entry for Jupiter. I just couldn't sit still while I was presenting it to the class. So, no, the distraction or inattention piece just wasn't there. It was always just the physical energy and the talking.

turns.doctor_question: Before age 12, did you also have a lot of trouble waiting your turn?
turns.patient_response:
Waiting my turn? Hmm... no, I don't think that was really an issue. I mean, I had—like I said before, I had all this energy, but I wasn't... I wasn't rude about it, if that makes sense. I understood the rules. 

I remember at recess, we played Four Square religiously. We had this huge blacktop behind the elementary school, and the maintenance guy, Mr. Henderson, had painted maybe six or seven courts in this bright yellow paint that was always peeling by the time spring rolled around. And there was always a huge line for the best court, the one near the big maple tree where there was actually a little bit of shade. I would stand in that line, and sure, I’d be bouncing on my toes, or maybe practicing my serving swing in the air, or just talking a mile a minute to whoever was in front of me—usually my best friend Sarah, she always wore these little plastic strawberry barrettes that clicked when she walked. But I never cut the line. I never jumped in before the person who got out was fully off the court. I knew exactly where my place was.

And it was the exact same way at home. We played a lot of board games on the weekends because my parents really believed in "family time" without the television on. Monopoly, Life, Sorry!... all of those. My older brother, David, he was always the banker in Monopoly, and he was so incredibly slow. He would count out the colorful bills, organizing them perfectly by denomination, making sure all the edges lined up. It honestly drove me crazy internally. I'd be sitting there tapping my little metal piece on the board—I always had to be the thimble, I just loved the texture of it—and I'd be squirming in my chair, practically vibrating while I waited for him to finish his turn so I could roll the dice. But I never reached over and grabbed the dice out of turn, and I never tried to go before he was completely finished. 

So, I guess the physical act of standing or sitting still while I waited was hard—my body always wanted to just go, go, go—but I didn't actually have trouble with the concept of waiting my turn. I didn't push ahead of people or anything like that.

And then at home... well, it’s mostly around dinner time. We always try to sit down together, my husband and our two teenagers, around the dining room table. I'm up and down, getting more water, checking the oven, or I'm just talking so fast and so much. I get so animated and I just keep going, and I end up dominating the conversation. My husband actually sat me down a few weeks ago—we were on the patio, having coffee—and he told me that family dinners have been getting really tense lately. It's not that I don't know how to do my job—I've been a buyer for a long time, I know these spreadsheets inside and out, I know what to look for—it's just these silly, careless little slips. And Jessica is so sweet about it, she never makes a big production out of it, she just highlights it in yellow and sends it back. But I know it creates extra work for her, and it just makes me feel like I'm losing my edge, you know? Like, how could I miss a simple freight charge when I've processed a thousand of these? turns.doctor_question: Do you also act without thinking, such as interrupting people or blurting things out before you mean to?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, goodness, yes. That is... yeah, that's actually a really big one for me. It happens constantly, especially when I think I know exactly where a conversation is going. My brain just sort of leaps ahead to the end of the sentence, and my mouth just follows right along with it before I can stop myself. 

Take my job, for instance. When I'm in vendor negotiations—which, like I was saying earlier with the spreadsheets, is just a massive part of what I do. We deal with so many suppliers, and some of these reps, they just take a very, very long time to get to the point. We have this one supplier in Ohio, they do our ceramic goods, and their main rep, Gary, he is a lovely man, but he speaks at a snail's pace. He'll be in the middle of asking a question about our Q3 volume commitments or pitching a new pricing tier, and I just... I jump right in with an answer before he has even finished the question. I'll blurt out our standard counteroffer because I'm just so eager to keep the meeting moving. But then, he'll finish his thought, and I'll realize that I completely missed an important qualifier he was about to add. He'll say something like, "...but that's only if we use the alternative freight carrier," which obviously changes the entire context of my answer. And then I have to backtrack and apologize, and it just makes me look a bit unpolished.

And it's not just at the office, either. I also do this volunteer thing—I mentor young women in STEM programs at the local community college. I started doing it a few years ago after I finished my bachelor's because I really believe in giving back, and I remember how intimidating those quantitative classes could be. Anyway, we have these mentoring sessions, usually on Tuesday evenings in this slightly drafty old library room they let us use. The girls will be asking me a question about career paths or how to handle a heavy course load, and they're usually a bit nervous, trying to find the right words. And instead of just sitting there and letting them work through it, I'll interrupt them. I'll just blurt out this whole piece of advice before they've finished speaking. And then they'll look at me kind of sideways, and I'll realize they were about to say, "...but my scholarship requires me to take this specific lab," or some other really important qualifier that completely changes the advice I should be giving them. 

I really don't mean to be rude or talk over people. It's just like I have the answer right there on the tip of my tongue, and it feels almost physically uncomfortable to hold it in. The thought is there and it just has to come out immediately, right in that exact second, before I've actually heard everything they have to say.

Oh, definitely. It’s not just the jumping out of my chair or the blurting things out. The distractibility is... well, it's really frustrating, actually, because it happens even when I'm really trying my hardest to focus.

And then the room gets quiet, and a few seconds later I realize I only caught the absolute last part of what they said, maybe the last three or four words. But then I realize I haven't processed a single word she's said for the last two minutes. I'll just catch the very tail end of it, like "...so what do you think I should do?" And I just sit there, totally blank, feeling like the worst mother in the world, having to admit that I need her to say it all over again. It’s just awful, having to constantly say, "I'm sorry, can you repeat that?" when I was staring right at them the entire time.

So, yes, I am constantly in motion, from the minute I wake up until my head finally hits the pillow.
